Mutating the aromatic residue to alanine removes the π platform and hence all the CH–π contacts, so binding collapses — direct evidence the interaction is load-bearing.

items.prompt: Using the worm-like-chain result ⟨R²⟩ = 2ℓ_pL − 2ℓ_p²(1 − e^(−L/ℓ_p)), (a) show the rod and coil limits, and (b) compute the RMS end-to-end distance of a 1000-bp DNA (L = 340 nm, ℓ_p = 50 nm).
choices: It is measured in solution at room temperature, so it samples the molecule's real conformational fluctuations — the output is an ensemble consistent with the restraints. The limit is molecular size: slow tumbling broadens lines, capping standard methods near 30–50 kDa without TROSY/deuteration.
Nucleation–elongation (a slow nucleation step followed by rapid fibril growth, often with secondary nucleation).

C = εε₀κ = εε₀/λ_D = (80 × 8.85×10⁻¹²)/(0.78×10⁻⁹) = (7.08×10⁻¹⁰)/(7.8×10⁻¹⁰) = 0.91 F/m². Convert: 1 F/m² = 100 µF/cm², so C ≈ 91 µF/cm². This large diffuse-layer capacitance (thin layer at high salt) is why the electrical double layer stores substantial charge per area and why cell-membrane and electrode interfaces have capacitances in the tens-of-µF/cm² range.

(a) For L ≪ ℓ_p expand e^(−L/ℓ_p) ≈ 1 − L/ℓ_p + L²/2ℓ_p², so 1−e^(−L/ℓ_p) ≈ L/ℓ_p − L²/2ℓ_p²; then ⟨R²⟩ ≈ 2ℓ_pL − 2ℓ_p²(L/ℓ_p − L²/2ℓ_p²) = 2ℓ_pL − 2ℓ_pL + L² = L² (rigid rod). For L ≫ ℓ_p the exponential → 0, so ⟨R²⟩ ≈ 2ℓ_pL (Gaussian coil, Kuhn length 2ℓ_p). (b) ⟨R²⟩ = 2(50)(340) − 2(50)²(1 − e^(−340/50)) = 34000 − 5000(1 − e^(−6.8)) = 34000 − 5000(0.99889) ≈ 29006 nm², so √⟨R²⟩ ≈ 170 nm — the 340 nm contour is coiled to about half its length.

items.prompt: A protein-nanoparticle suspension has a zeta potential of −40 mV and stays dispersed for weeks. After adding salt the zeta potential rises to −8 mV and the particles aggregate overnight. Explain the connection.
choices: Zeta potential measures the effective charge felt at the slipping plane, which drives electrostatic repulsion between particles. At −40 mV the mutual repulsion is strong enough to overcome van der Waals attraction, so particles stay apart (stable colloid, roughly |ζ| > 25–30 mV). Adding salt compresses the Debye screening layer and lowers |ζ| to 8 mV; the repulsive barrier collapses, van der Waals attraction wins, and the particles aggregate. So ζ is the practical dial for colloidal stability.

Stickers are the multivalent attractive motifs that drive association; spacers are the flexible linkers connecting them and tuning solubility/solvent quality. Scaffolds are the components whose multivalent interactions drive phase separation; clients are molecules that partition into the condensate without driving its formation.
If it increases entropy enough that TΔS outweighs ΔU, ΔF is still negative — entropy can pay for energy.

items.prompt: Using Helmholtz–Smoluchowski μ_e = εε₀ζ/η for a large particle in water (ε = 80, ε₀ = 8.85×10⁻¹² F/m, η = 8.9×10⁻⁴ Pa·s), compute the electrophoretic mobility for ζ = −30 mV, and give its sign and meaning.
choices: k = 4πDR = 4π×(10⁻⁹)×(10⁻⁹) ≈ 1.26×10⁻¹⁷ m³/s per pair. Multiply by Avogadro's number (6.02×10²³ mol⁻¹) and 1000 L/m³ to get molar units: 1.26×10⁻¹⁷ × 6.02×10²³ × 10³ ≈ 7.6×10⁹ M⁻¹s⁻¹. This ~10¹⁰ M⁻¹s⁻¹ ceiling is the diffusion limit; measured on-rates near it mean binding is gated by how fast partners meet, not by any chemical barrier.

εε₀ = 80×8.85×10⁻¹² = 7.08×10⁻¹⁰ F/m. Then μ_e = (7.08×10⁻¹⁰ × (−0.030))/(8.9×10⁻⁴) = (−2.12×10⁻¹¹)/(8.9×10⁻⁴) ≈ −2.4×10⁻⁸ m²·V⁻¹·s⁻¹. The negative sign means the particle carries net negative charge and migrates toward the positive electrode (anode); its speed in a field of, say, 100 V/m would be v = μ_e·E ≈ 2.4×10⁻⁶ m/s = 2.4 µm/s.
The membrane potential Δψ and the transmembrane pH difference. The coupling intermediate is the proton gradient itself (proton-motive force), not a chemical intermediate.

(a) ⟨u²⟩ = B/(8π²) = 20/78.96 = 0.253 Å², so √⟨u²⟩ = 0.50 Å. (b) 3-D RMSF = √(3×0.253) = √0.760 = 0.87 Å. (c) From equipartition k⟨u²⟩ = k_BT: with ⟨u²⟩ = 0.253 Å² = 0.253×10⁻²⁰ m² and k_BT = 1.38×10⁻²³×300 = 4.14×10⁻²¹ J, k = k_BT/⟨u²⟩ = 4.14×10⁻²¹/(0.253×10⁻²⁰) ≈ 1.6 N/m — a soft effective spring, consistent with a loosely restrained atom.

items.prompt: Urea destabilizes proteins while the osmolyte TMAO stabilizes them. Using the idea of preferential interaction, explain both, and say what the sign of the m-value is for each with respect to unfolding.
choices: Unfolding exposes a lot of new surface. Urea interacts favorably with that newly exposed backbone and side chains, so it preferentially accumulates around the unfolded state (ΔΓ > 0); by Wyman linkage this lowers the free energy of U relative to N, driving unfolding — a positive m-value for unfolding, destabilizing. TMAO is preferentially excluded from the backbone (osmophobic effect), so it raises the free energy of the more-exposed unfolded state, increasing ΔG_unf and stabilizing the protein. Its effect has the opposite sign, favoring the folded state.

Gamma_(i->f) = (2 pi / hbar) |<f|V|i>|^2 rho(E_f). The two factors are (1) the squared coupling matrix element |<f|V|i>|^2 - how strongly the perturbation connects the initial and final states - and (2) the density of final states rho(E_f) - how many states are available to accept the transition at the final energy. The coupling factor controls, for example, spectroscopic absorption intensity: it is the squared transition dipole |<f|mu|i>|^2, so a symmetry that makes the dipole vanish gives a forbidden (weak) line. In Marcus electron transfer the same factor becomes the squared donor-acceptor electronic coupling |H_DA|^2. The density-of-states factor controls the other half: in Marcus theory it is the Franck-Condon-weighted density of vibrational states (the Gaussian activation term), and in NMR/EPR relaxation it is the spectral density J(omega) of molecular tumbling evaluated at the resonance frequency, which is why relaxation rates depend on the correlation time of motion.

(a) At the midpoint ΔG_unf = 0, so 0 = ΔG° − m·C_m ⇒ C_m = ΔG°/m = 5.0/1.0 = 5.0 M. (b) With a shared m, ΔΔG = m·ΔC_m = 1.0×(5.0 − 3.0) = 2.0 kcal/mol. The mutant is destabilized by 2.0 kcal/mol — it takes 2 M less urea to reach its unfolding midpoint. This linear-extrapolation reading of ΔΔG from a shift in C_m is the standard way mutational stability effects are measured.

Desolvation (burial in a low-dielectric interior), nearby fixed charges (favorable or unfavorable), and hydrogen bonding to the ionizable group. All are electrostatic contributions to the charged-vs-neutral free energy.

items.prompt: A protein has ΔG°(H₂O) = 5.0 kcal/mol and unfolds with m = 1.0 kcal·mol⁻¹·M⁻¹ in urea. (a) Find the midpoint concentration C_m. (b) A point mutant has the same m but denatures at C_m = 3.0 M. What is ΔΔG between wild type and mutant?
choices: (a) At the midpoint ΔG_unf = 0, so 0 = ΔG° − m·C_m ⇒ C_m = ΔG°/m = 5.0/1.0 = 5.0 M. (b) With a shared m, ΔΔG = m·ΔC_m = 1.0×(5.0 − 3.0) = 2.0 kcal/mol. The mutant is destabilized by 2.0 kcal/mol — it takes 2 M less urea to reach its unfolding midpoint. This linear-extrapolation reading of ΔΔG from a shift in C_m is the standard way mutational stability effects are measured.

Umbrella sampling adds biasing potentials to force the simulation to sample high-energy regions along a reaction coordinate in overlapping windows. WHAM reweights and stitches the biased histograms together into the unbiased potential of mean force (free-energy profile).

A classical hydrogen bond (e.g. O–H···O) is dominated by electrostatics and is relatively strong (~5 kcal/mol) and directional. A CH–π interaction uses a weak C–H donor and an aromatic π cloud as acceptor, and it is dominated instead by dispersion (London) forces with only a small electrostatic/charge-transfer part, so it is much weaker — roughly 1–2.5 kcal/mol per contact — and only mildly directional. Its geometric signature is the C–H pointing toward the ring centroid with the hydrogen sitting about 2.5–3.5 Å above the aromatic plane.

Any of: lost chemical/atomic detail; the CG potential is a free energy, so it is temperature- and concentration-dependent and may not transfer between conditions; the dynamics are artificially accelerated, so simulated time is not physical time; entropy is softened. Coarse-grained kinetics in particular must be reinterpreted.

items.prompt: In a refined protein crystal structure, the buried core atoms have B-factors around 10 Å² while a surface loop shows 60 Å². What does this tell you, and why does cooling the crystal to 100 K generally improve the data?
choices: The B-factor is proportional to each atom's mean-square displacement (B = 8π²⟨u²⟩), so the core atoms are rigid and well-ordered while the surface loop is highly mobile or disordered — exactly where the electron density is weakest. Cooling to 100 K lowers thermal motion (⟨u²⟩ = k_BT/k drops with T), which shrinks the B-factors, sharpens the high-angle reflections, pushes resolution higher, and also greatly reduces radiation damage during data collection.

λ is the free-energy cost of rearranging the nuclei and surrounding solvent from the reactant to the product geometry without moving the electron. The rate is maximal (barrierless) when the driving force exactly matches it: −ΔG° = λ.
About +61 mV (≈ 61 mV per tenfold ratio for z = +1).

ln(K₂/K₁) = −(ΔH°/R)(1/T₂ − 1/T₁). Here −ΔH°/R = +50000/8.314 = 6014 K, and (1/310 − 1/300) = −1.075×10⁻⁴ K⁻¹, so ln(K₂/K₁) = 6014 × (−1.075×10⁻⁴) = −0.647, giving K₂/K₁ = e^{−0.647} ≈ 0.52. The equilibrium constant roughly halves: heating an exothermic reaction shifts it backward, the quantitative form of Le Chatelier and the exact mirror of the Arrhenius Q10 (which instead nearly doubles the rate).

items.prompt: An atom is refined with an isotropic B-factor of 20 Å². (a) Compute its one-dimensional RMS displacement √⟨u²⟩. (b) Compute its three-dimensional RMSF, √(3⟨u²⟩). (c) Treating it as a harmonic oscillator at 300 K, estimate the effective spring constant k.
choices: 4RT_m² = 4·(8.314×10⁻³)·(330)² = 0.033256·108900 ≈ 3.62×10³ kJ·K·mol⁻¹. Times C_p,max: 3.62×10³·44 ≈ 1.594×10⁵. Divide by ΔH_cal = 400: ΔH_vH ≈ 398 kJ/mol. The ratio ΔH_cal/ΔH_vH = 400/398 ≈ 1.0, so the transition behaves as a single cooperative two-state unfolding of a monomer (no resolvable intermediates or oligomeric coupling).

(a) ⟨u²⟩ = B/(8π²) = 20/78.96 = 0.253 Å², so √⟨u²⟩ = 0.50 Å. (b) 3-D RMSF = √(3×0.253) = √0.760 = 0.87 Å. (c) From equipartition k⟨u²⟩ = k_BT: with ⟨u²⟩ = 0.253 Å² = 0.253×10⁻²⁰ m² and k_BT = 1.38×10⁻²³×300 = 4.14×10⁻²¹ J, k = k_BT/⟨u²⟩ = 4.14×10⁻²¹/(0.253×10⁻²⁰) ≈ 1.6 N/m — a soft effective spring, consistent with a loosely restrained atom.

Separating variables, dR/R = −k_off dt ⇒ R(t) = R_0 e^(−k_off·t): dissociation is a single exponential. The half-life is t_½ = ln2/k_off = 0.693/0.01 ≈ 69 s. The affinity is K_d = k_off/k_on = 0.01/(1×10⁶) = 1×10⁻⁸ M = 10 nM.
Backbone dihedrals φ and ψ; only some combinations avoid steric clashes between atoms.

items.prompt: Why can two like-charged groups on a protein sit close together in water when the same charges would repel violently in a vacuum, and what single quantity captures that difference?
choices: Π = cRT = (300 mol/m³)(8.314 J/mol·K)(310 K) ≈ 7.7×10⁵ Pa ≈ 7.6 atm. A red cell in pure water faces this large inward osmotic drive: water rushes in, the cell swells, and — having no rigid wall — it bursts (hemolysis). This is why intravenous fluids are made isotonic (~300 mOsm) to match plasma.

Water has a high relative permittivity (ε ≈ 80), so its polarizable dipoles reorient to oppose the field and cut the Coulomb interaction roughly 80-fold. The quantity that captures this is the Bjerrum length ℓ_B = e²/(4πεε₀k_BT) ≈ 0.71 nm in water — the separation at which two elementary charges interact with just k_BT. Beyond a nanometre or so their bare repulsion is already comparable to thermal energy, so it no longer dominates.

ν = gμ_B B / h = (2.0023)(9.274×10⁻²⁴ J/T)(0.35 T) / (6.626×10⁻³⁴ J·s). Numerator = 2.0023 × 9.274×10⁻²⁴ × 0.35 ≈ 6.50×10⁻²⁴ J; dividing by h gives ν ≈ 9.8×10⁹ Hz ≈ 9.8 GHz — the X-band microwave frequency, consistent with standard EPR spectrometers.

Function often requires liquid-like fast exchange, while aberrant hardening (liquid-to-solid maturation/ageing) is linked to pathological aggregation in neurodegeneration. You measure internal dynamics by FRAP (recovery rate) and viscoelasticity by active microrheology, and map phase behavior by controlled in-vitro reconstitution — matching the observable to the material property.

items.prompt: Starting from Coulomb's law, find the electrostatic energy of two elementary charges separated by r = 1 nm (a) in vacuum and (b) in water (ε = 80), and express each as a multiple of k_BT at 300 K. (e = 1.60×10⁻¹⁹ C, ε₀ = 8.85×10⁻¹² F/m, k_BT = 4.14×10⁻²¹ J.)
choices: Electrons flow from low to high reduction potential (NADH to O₂); the released free energy is stored as a transmembrane electrochemical proton gradient (proton-motive force).

The pair energy is U = e²/(4πεε₀r). Compute the vacuum case: e² = 2.566×10⁻³⁸ C²; 4πε₀ = 1.113×10⁻¹⁰; times r = 1×10⁻⁹ gives 1.113×10⁻¹⁹, so U_vac = 2.566×10⁻³⁸/1.113×10⁻¹⁹ = 2.31×10⁻¹⁹ J = 1.44 eV = 2.31×10⁻¹⁹/4.14×10⁻²¹ ≈ 56 k_BT. (b) In water divide by ε = 80: U_water = 2.89×10⁻²¹ J ≈ 0.70 k_BT. The 0.70 factor is just r shrinking below the Bjerrum length ℓ_B = 0.71 nm — at r = ℓ_B the energy would be exactly 1 k_BT.

K is the fixed ratio of products to reactants (each raised to its stoichiometric power) reached at equilibrium. It is related to the standard free-energy change by ΔG° = −RT ln K, equivalently K = exp(−ΔG°/RT).
The substrate concentration giving half the maximum rate (V_max/2).

items.prompt: Why is a single van der Waals contact almost negligible, yet van der Waals forces are decisive for whether a protein folds or a membrane holds together?
choices: Statistical mechanics counts microstates: the multiplicity of a macrostate is a product of factorials, and entropy is S = k_B ln Ω. A sum of discrete log-factorials cannot be differentiated, so you cannot find the most probable distribution. Stirling's approximation, ln N! ≈ N ln N − N, turns each factorial into a smooth, differentiable function of N. Only then can you extremize ln Ω (with Lagrange multipliers for fixed energy and particle number) to derive the Boltzmann distribution and the partition function. It is the mathematical bridge from combinatorics to thermodynamics.

ΔpKa = ΔΔG_elec/(2.303·RT), where ΔΔG_elec is the change in free energy of forming the charged state inside the protein relative to in solution. A positive electrostatic penalty for the charge of an acid raises its pKa; stabilizing it lowers the pKa.

The sign of the ring's quadrupole moment Q_zz flips. Benzene is π-basic with Q_zz < 0 (its faces are electron-rich/negative), so it attracts cations (cation–π). Hanging electron-withdrawing groups on the ring — six fluorines in hexafluorobenzene, or ring nitrogens in triazine — reverses the quadrupole to Q_zz > 0 (π-acidic, positive faces), so the ring now attracts an anion over its centroid. The leading electrostatic term is the charge–quadrupole interaction, E ≈ qQ_zz/r³, and it is reinforced by anion-induced polarization of the ring.

One pairwise contact has a well depth of only about 0.1 kcal/mol — far below the thermal energy k_BT ≈ 0.6 kcal/mol at room temperature, so on its own it is easily broken. But the interactions are additive and short-ranged, so a tightly packed protein core or a lipid bilayer stacks thousands of them; the sum reaches tens of kcal/mol. Good packing (many atoms at their r_min) is what turns a weak universal force into a strong structural glue.

items.prompt: For the Lennard-Jones potential U(r)=4ε[(σ/r)¹²−(σ/r)⁶], show that the minimum is at r_min=2^{1/6}σ and that U(r_min)=−ε.
choices: Binding increases the mass (and thus the refractive index) near the gold surface, shifting the plasmon-resonance angle; the response (in RU) is proportional to bound mass. Fitting the sensorgram's association and dissociation phases yields the on-rate k_on and off-rate k_off, whose ratio is the affinity K_d = k_off/k_on.

Set dU/dr=0. Write x=σ/r, so U=4ε(x¹²−x⁶). Then dU/dr=(dU/dx)(dx/dr) and dx/dr=−σ/r²≠0, so the minimum needs dU/dx=0: 4ε(12x¹¹−6x⁵)=0 ⇒ x⁵(12x⁶−6)=0 ⇒ x⁶=1/2 ⇒ x=(1/2)^{1/6}. Since x=σ/r, r_min=σ/x=σ·2^{1/6}≈1.122σ. Substitute x⁶=1/2: U=4ε[(x⁶)²−x⁶]=4ε[(1/2)²−(1/2)]=4ε(1/4−1/2)=4ε(−1/4)=−ε. So the well depth is exactly ε.
Mobile counter-ions screen charges; λ_D decreases as ionic strength increases (∝ 1/√I).

Detailed balance gives W_{i→j}/W_{j→i} = P_j/P_i = e^{−(E_j−E_i)/k_BT} = e^{−2} = 0.135. So P_j/P_i = 0.135 (the higher-energy state j is less populated). The reverse rate is W_{j→i} = W_{i→j} / 0.135 = 1×10⁶ / 0.135 = 7.4×10⁶ s⁻¹ — downhill transitions are faster, exactly enough to keep the matched fluxes P_i W_{i→j} = P_j W_{j→i} balanced.

items.prompt: A hydrogen bond in vacuum can be worth 2–8 kcal/mol, yet each backbone hydrogen bond contributes only a fraction of that to protein stability. Why?
choices: The pair energy is U = e²/(4πεε₀r). Compute the vacuum case: e² = 2.566×10⁻³⁸ C²; 4πε₀ = 1.113×10⁻¹⁰; times r = 1×10⁻⁹ gives 1.113×10⁻¹⁹, so U_vac = 2.566×10⁻³⁸/1.113×10⁻¹⁹ = 2.31×10⁻¹⁹ J = 1.44 eV = 2.31×10⁻¹⁹/4.14×10⁻²¹ ≈ 56 k_BT. (b) In water divide by ε = 80: U_water = 2.89×10⁻²¹ J ≈ 0.70 k_BT. The 0.70 factor is just r shrinking below the Bjerrum length ℓ_B = 0.71 nm — at r = ℓ_B the energy would be exactly 1 k_BT.

With P_Na = P_Cl = 0, every Na/Cl term vanishes and V_m = (RT/F)·ln([K]_o/[K]_i) = E_K — the single-ion Nernst result. For the two-ion case the numerator = 1×4 + 0.04×145 = 9.8 and the denominator = 1×140 + 0.04×12 ≈ 140.5, so V_m = 26.7·ln(9.8/140.5) = 26.7×(−2.66) ≈ −71 mV. The small Na⁺ leak (P_Na/P_K = 0.04) pulls the resting potential ~20 mV positive of pure E_K, exactly as real neurons sit.

The swollen coil has the larger R_g because its mass is spread farther from the center. With chain length, a compact globule keeps constant density so R_g ∝ N^(1/3), an ideal (theta-solvent) coil scales as R_g ∝ N^(1/2), and a self-avoiding swollen coil in good solvent scales as R_g ∝ N^ν with ν ≈ 0.588. So measuring how R_g grows with N distinguishes collapsed, ideal, and swollen states.

In water the donor and acceptor can hydrogen-bond either to each other or to surrounding water molecules. When a protein folds and forms an intramolecular hydrogen bond, it must give up the hydrogen bonds those groups had made to water. The two roughly cancel, so the NET stabilisation is only a few tenths to ~1–2 kcal/mol per bond. This near-cancellation is a major reason proteins are only marginally stable overall.

items.prompt: What single geometric feature of the hydrogen bond makes it, rather than van der Waals or generic electrostatics, the force that encodes specific molecular structures like the α-helix and Watson–Crick base pairs?
choices: Inversely on both: D = kT/(6πηr) — bigger or more viscous means slower diffusion.

You need several steps per oscillation, so Δt ≈ 1 fs (about a tenth of the fastest period); larger makes the integrator unstable and the energy blow up. To reach ~2 fs you constrain (freeze) the X–H bonds with SHAKE or LINCS, removing the fastest motion so a bigger step stays stable.

AFM accesses higher forces (tens of pN to nN) and stiffer probes, so it suits strong unfolding events and receptor–ligand bond rupture, plus topographic imaging; optical tweezers offer finer force resolution (sub-pN) for delicate, low-force measurements like motor stepping.

Its directionality. The partially positive hydrogen wants to point straight at the acceptor's lone pair, so the D–H···A angle prefers to be near 180° and the D···A distance sits in a narrow ~2.7–3.0 Å window. Van der Waals attraction is isotropic (no preferred direction) and bare electrostatics is only weakly directional, so neither can enforce a precise geometry. The hydrogen bond's angular pickiness is what lets it act like a lock-and-key, aligning helical turns and pairing A with T and G with C reproducibly.

items.prompt: In the continuity equation ∂ρ/∂t + ∇·J = s, what does a positive ∇·J at a point physically mean, and what happens to ρ there if s = 0?
choices: k_BT — the thermal energy, ≈ 0.6 kcal/mol (2.5 kJ/mol) at 310 K.

A positive divergence ∇·J means net outflow — more of the quantity is leaving the neighbourhood of that point than arriving (the point acts as a spreading source of flux). With no source (s = 0), the continuity equation gives ∂ρ/∂t = −∇·J < 0, so the density at that point must decrease over time. The stuff is draining away because more flows out than in.
The Helmholtz free energy F = U − TS = −kT ln Z.

The ratio changes by exp(−ΔΔG/RT). With RT ≈ 0.59 kcal/mol, ΔΔG/RT = 1.4/0.59 ≈ 2.3 = ln 10, so K drops by a factor of ≈ 10 — the fold is ~10× less populated. (≈1.4 kcal/mol per decade is the recurring 'one log unit' rule of thumb.)

items.prompt: Combine the continuity equation (no sources) with Fick's first law J = −D∇c to derive Fick's second law, and state what physical assumption lets D come outside the derivative.
choices: E = 1/(1+(r/R₀)⁶). R₀, the Förster radius, is the donor–acceptor separation at which transfer efficiency is 50% (typically 2–6 nm).
Poisson's equation (∇²φ = −ρ/εε₀) and the Boltzmann distribution for the mobile-ion concentrations (nᵢ ∝ e^(−qᵢφ/kT)).

Continuity with s = 0 is ∂c/∂t = −∇·J. Substitute Fick's first law J = −D∇c: ∂c/∂t = −∇·(−D∇c) = ∇·(D∇c). If D is spatially uniform (constant), it pulls out of the divergence: ∂c/∂t = D∇·(∇c) = D∇²c — Fick's second law, the diffusion equation. The key assumption is a constant diffusion coefficient; if D varies with position or concentration, it must stay inside as ∇·(D∇c).

A free molecule has 3 translational (quadratic kinetic) degrees of freedom, so ⟨KE⟩ = 3 × ½k_BT = (3/2)k_BT; for a mole U = (3/2)RT and C_V = (3/2)R ≈ 12.5 J/mol/K (the monatomic-gas value). A vibration adds 2 quadratic terms (kinetic + potential) → k_BT each when active, but equipartition is classical: a degree of freedom only absorbs its full share when its quantum spacing ħω ≲ k_BT. A stiff bond has ħω ≫ k_BT at 300 K, so it is 'frozen out' and stores almost no thermal energy — the same reason solids fall below the Dulong–Petit 3R heat capacity as they cool.

items.prompt: You have a charged membrane in a dilute salt solution. What happens to the thickness of its diffuse double layer, and to the reach of its surface potential, if you raise the salt concentration tenfold?
choices: The diffuse layer thins. Its thickness is the Debye length λ_D = κ⁻¹, which scales as 1/√(ionic strength), so a tenfold increase in salt shrinks it by √10 ≈ 3.2×. The surface potential ψ(x) ≈ ψ₀e^(−κx) therefore decays over a shorter distance — the membrane's electrostatic reach into solution is compressed. This is why high salt screens electrostatic interactions and can collapse colloidal or membrane repulsion.

The pure radiative lifetime is τ_rad = 1/k_r with k_r = A. When nonradiative channels exist, the excited state decays at the total rate k_r + k_nr, so the observed lifetime is τ_obs = 1/(k_r + k_nr) < τ_rad. FRET adds a transfer rate k_FRET to the denominator: τ_obs = 1/(k_r + k_nr + k_FRET), so energy transfer shortens the donor lifetime — the basis of lifetime FRET. The fluorescence quantum yield is Φ = k_r/(k_r + k_nr), the fraction of excitations that leave as emitted photons.
The contour distance over which a polymer's backbone direction stays correlated (it 'forgets' its orientation beyond it).

items.prompt: In the low-potential limit the diffuse layer acts as a capacitor with areal capacitance C = εε₀κ. Estimate C for water (ε = 80) at physiological ionic strength (Debye length λ_D ≈ 0.78 nm), and give it in µF/cm². (ε₀ = 8.85×10⁻¹² F/m.)

items.prompt: The simple Hunter–Sanders quadrupole model predicts the preferred geometries of aromatic stacking well, yet high-level SAPT calculations say the *binding energy* of the benzene dimer is dominated by dispersion. Are these statements in conflict?

The quadrupole electrostatics is smaller in magnitude but strongly *orientation-dependent*, so it decides *which* geometry is lowest in energy — it selects the shape while dispersion supplies the glue. The Hunter–Sanders model captures the geometry-selecting electrostatics; SAPT captures the full energy breakdown. Together they say: dispersion holds the rings together, quadrupole electrostatics chooses the offset/T arrangement.

The master equation describes a system hopping randomly between discrete states (a continuous-time Markov process). For each state i it balances probability gain and loss: dP_i/dt = Σ_j (W_{ji}P_j − W_{ij}P_i), where W_{ij} is the rate from i to j. The stationary state is reached when every state's net flow is zero (dP_i/dt = 0) — incoming and outgoing probability balance overall. Detailed balance is stronger: it requires every individual pair of states to balance, W_{ij}P_i^{eq} = W_{ji}P_j^{eq}, so there are no circulating probability currents. Every detailed-balance state is stationary, but a stationary state can carry steady cyclic currents (a nonequilibrium steady state, as in molecular motors) without satisfying detailed balance.

items.prompt: Lectins and glycoside hydrolases almost always have a tryptophan or tyrosine in their sugar-binding site, and mutating it to alanine abolishes binding. Explain, in terms of CH–π interactions, why aromatic platforms are so well suited to recognizing carbohydrates in water.
choices: Model a vibrating bond as a quantum harmonic oscillator with states |n>. For small displacements the dipole moment is linear in the coordinate, mu(x) approx mu_0 + (d(mu)/dx) x, so the transition dipole between states |n> and |m> is mu_mn = mu_0 <m|n> + (d(mu)/dx) <m|x|n>. The first term vanishes for m != n by orthogonality, so intensity comes from <m|x|n>. Write the position operator in ladder form x = sqrt(hbar/2 m omega) (a + a-dagger), where a|n> = sqrt(n)|n-1> and a-dagger|n> = sqrt(n+1)|n+1>. Then <m|x|n> = sqrt(hbar/2 m omega) [ sqrt(n) <m|n-1> + sqrt(n+1) <m|n+1> ], which is nonzero only when m = n - 1 or m = n + 1. Hence the transition dipole is nonzero only for Delta-v = m - n = +/- 1: a harmonic vibration absorbs or emits one quantum at a time. It also shows the second corollary - if d(mu)/dx = 0 (a symmetric, nonpolar stretch) the whole matrix element vanishes and the mode is IR-inactive, no matter the level spacing.

A sharp, switch-like input/output relationship (effective Hill coefficient much greater than 1), turning a graded signal into a near-digital response. Mechanisms include multistep phosphorylation, zero-order ultrasensitivity (Goldbeter–Koshland), and molecular titration.

It means the unfolding is not a single two-state transition. ΔH_cal (the area) is the total heat actually absorbed, while ΔH_vH (from the peak sharpness) is the heat a single cooperative equilibrium would need. A ratio above 1 means the observed transition is broader than one two-state step — the molecule unfolds as several independent domains or through folding intermediates, each melting over its own narrow range, so the summed area exceeds the single-equilibrium prediction.

A pyranose sugar is amphipathic: one face of the ring presents a patch of nonpolar C–H groups. These are good (mildly acidic) CH–π donors, and an aromatic side chain (Trp indole, Tyr phenol) provides a broad, flat, polarizable π platform on which that C–H face can lie, forming several CH–π contacts at once. Although each contact is weak (~1–2 kcal/mol), they act cooperatively and add up to meaningful affinity. Crucially, because both partners are relatively nonpolar the interaction carries a small desolvation penalty, so it survives well in water where polar hydrogen bonds to the sugar's OH groups are heavily competed by solvent. Mutating the aromatic residue to alanine removes the π platform and hence all the CH–π contacts, so binding collapses — direct evidence the interaction is load-bearing.
